nameStory: The Southern House Spider gets its name from its preference for living around human dwellings, especially in the warmer southern states where it's most common. Despite being called 'southern,' this wandering spider has been making its way north and can occasionally be found in New England homes and buildings.
description: The Southern House Spider is a large, impressive spider that can stretch nearly 2 inches across with legs extended. Males and females look dramatically different - males are brownish and leggy with a more compact body, while females are dark brown to black with bulkier, more robust bodies. Both have a distinctive velvety, fine gray hair covering their abdomens that gives them a soft, fuzzy appearance.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Males have exceptionally long, slender legs and compact bodies, while females are more robust and stocky with shorter legs relative to body size

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The abdomen feels and looks velvety due to fine, light gray hairs that cover it like soft plush fabric

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large spiders reaching up to 2 inches across with legs extended, making them noticeably bigger than most house spiders

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Females build distinctive radial webs around cracks and crevices that feel less sticky than typical spider webs, more like fine velcro

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Males wander boldly across surfaces and will crawl directly over objects (including people) in their path without hesitation

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Males lack the distinctive violin-shaped marking of brown recluse spiders and have unusually long, slender pedipalps (feeding appendages near the mouth)

habitat: In New England, Southern House Spiders are most likely found in and around buildings, particularly in basements, garages, sheds, and other structures that provide cracks and crevices for web-building. They prefer warm, sheltered spots near human activity where insects are abundant. Look for them around foundations, window frames, and other architectural features that create the crevices these spiders need.

seasonality.spring: Males begin wandering more actively as temperatures warm, often appearing indoors as they search for mates and food.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both males and females are most active. Males are most likely to be encountered wandering at night.
seasonality.fall: Males continue wandering behavior into early fall, while females focus on web maintenance and egg production in their crevice hideouts.
seasonality.winter: Both sexes become less active and retreat deeper into warm crevices and sheltered areas, particularly in heated buildings.

funFact: Southern House Spiders don't make sticky webs like most spiders - instead, they use their legs like tiny combs to fray their silk into microscopic tangles that work like biological velcro, trapping insects by snagging their legs rather than gluing them down.
confusionNotes: Male Southern House Spiders are often mistaken for the venomous Brown Recluse because of their similar brown coloration and body structure. However, Southern House Spiders are typically larger, lack the violin-shaped marking on their back, and have noticeably longer, more slender leg-like feeding appendages near their mouth. Memory trick: 'Southern house spiders are bigger and bolder - brown recluse spiders are smaller and shyer.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'Southern' House Spider, climate change and human transportation have allowed this species to expand northward, which is why it occasionally appears in New England despite being far from its traditional range. The scientific name was recently changed from Filistata hibernalis to Kukulcania hibernalis, so you may see it listed under either name in older field guides.
compareHints: The Southern House Spider is the only member of its genus found in North America, making it unique among crevice weavers in the region. It can be distinguished from other large house spiders by its distinctive cribellate web structure (non-sticky, velcro-like silk) and the extreme sexual dimorphism between males and females. Most other large house spiders in New England produce traditional sticky webs and show less dramatic differences between sexes.
